newsitem.title: JAPAN: Kawasaki Steel develops zinc dust recovery method.
newsitem.headline: Kawasaki Steel develops zinc dust recovery method.

text.p: Kawasaki Steel said on Thursday it had developed a new technology to recover zinc from electric steel furnace dust and plans a feasibility study next year on a commercial plant that could begin operating as early as 1999.
He said the company is mulling a plant that could process 36,000 tonnes per year of the dust, which is 20 to 30 percent zinc, at a cost of less than 12,000 yen ($106) per tonne.

The plant would recover 100 percent of the zinc in the dust, which is produced by electric furnace, or scrap-based, steelmaking. Japan's electric furnace steelmakers produce about 500,000 tonnes of dust per year, the spokesman said.
He added that processing dust at Japan's zinc refiners currently costs 20,000 yen ($176) per tonne of dust with zinc recovery rates of only about 65 percent.

He also said the plant, which would cost less than 3 billion yen ($26.5 million) to build, would offer lower processing costs and higher recovery rates than technologies developed by Horsehead Resource Development Co and a joint project between Japan's Aichi Steel Works and Toyota Motor Corp.

Kawasaki's process heats furnace dust to 1,500 to 2,000 degrees centigrade, separating zinc, which is carried with furnace gases through a vent at the top of the vessel, from iron and slag, which can be used as feed for steel or cement making, the spokesman said.
The recovered zinc, with a purity of 60 percent or better, could be fed into a pyrometallurgical refining process.

The spokesman said Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry granted Kawasaki a three-year subsidy, beginning in April 1995, covering about two-thirds of the 330 million yen ($2.92 million) cost of a pilot plant that can process 10 tonnes of dust per day. The plant has successfully completed runs of up to three days, he said.

In recent years electric furnace steelmakers have sought cheap and effective technologies to deal with the rising amount of zinc in steel scrap, as zinc-coated galvanised steel has become popular among car and appliance manufacturers for its anti-corrosion and anti-rust properties. -- Tokyo Commodity Desk, 81-3-3432-6179
